i). Respondent no.1 in his written statement denied all the averments made in the claim petition except the occurrence of accident.
It is admitted that the claimant was going on the offending vehicle as a helper.

It is stated that the vehicle was proceeding towards Ashoka Foam Factory Mengi Nagla Faridpur, Bareilly, U.P from Old Seemapuri, Delhi and when it reached near Navadiya Jhada, Devsthan, U.P, all of a sudden, a Nilgai (blue bull) came in front of it and the balance of the vehicle was disturbed and the vehicle collided. As per the respondent no.1, he was driving at a normal speed with proper care and caution but due to the sudden surface of Boselaphus Tragocamelus (Nilgai), the accident occurred.

ii). Respondent no.3/ insurance company has also denied the claim of the petitioner and contended that the petition is not maintainable as there is no FIR or charge-sheet alleging any negligence against the driver of the insured vehicle.

My findings on the issues are as under:-
ISSUE NO.1

Whether petitioner suffered injuries during the accident occurred on 27/28.01.2019 at 12.30 mid night near Navadiya Jhada, Devsthan, U.P, within the jurisdiction of PS Bithri Chainpur, Bareilly, U.P. due to rash and negligent driving of the vehicle bearing no. DK1LAA- 3446 being driven by respondent no.1/ driver?
OPP 8.
It is settled proposition of law that in an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine-qua-non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of the preponderance of probabilities.
Holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.

Reference may be made to the judgments titled as New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v.
Sakshi Bhutani & Others., MAC APP. No. 550/2011 decided on 02.07.2012, Bimla Devi & Others v.
Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Others (2009) 13 SC 530, Parmeshwari v. Amirchand ______________________________________________________________________ MACT no. 195/2019; Saleem v. Sageer Ahmad & Ors. Page 6 & Others 2011 (1) SCR 1096 & Mangla Ram v. Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. & Others 2018, Law Suit (SC) 303.

sentences.text: 'Negligence' is failure to take proper care which a reasonable man would have taken under the circumstances.
What amounts to negligence depends on the facts of each particular case.
It may consist in omitting to do something which ought to be done or in doing something which ought to be done either in a different manner or not at all.
Where there is no duty to exercise care, negligence in the popular sense has no legal consequence.
Where there is a duty to exercise care, reasonable care must be taken to avoid acts or omissions which can be reasonably foreseen to be likely to cause physical injury to persons or property.

The degree of care required in the particular case depends on the surrounding circumstances, and may vary according to the amount of the risk to be encountered and to the magnitude of the prospective injury.

The duty of care is owed only to those persons who are in the area of foreseeable danger; the fact that the act of the defendant violated his duty of care to a third person does not enable the plaintiff who is also injured by the same act to claim unless he is also within the area of foreseeable danger.
The same act or omission may accordingly in some circumstances involve liability as being negligent, although in other circumstances it will not do so.

The material considerations are the absence of care which is on the part of the defendant owed to the plaintiff in the circumstances of the case and damage suffered by the plaintiff, together with a demonstrable relation of cause and effect between the two.

4 ______________________________________________________________________ MACT no. 195/2019; Saleem v. Sageer Ahmad & Ors. Page 7 10.

Negligence is conduct which falls below the standard established for the protection of others against unreasonable risk of harm, this standard of conduct is ordinarily measured by what the reasonable man of ordinary prudence would do under the circumstances.

In order to objectify the law's abstractions like "care", "reasonableness" or "foreseeability" the man of ordinary prudence was invented as a model of the standard of conduct to which all men are required to conform.
11. "Reckless" means "careless", regardless or heedless of the possible harmful consequences of one's acts.

It presupposes that if thought was given to the matter by the doer before the act was done, it would have been apparent to him that there was a real risk of its having the relevant harmful consequences; but, granted this, recklessness covers a whole range of states of mind from failing to give any thought at all to whether or not there is any risk of those harmful consequences, to recognising the existence of the risk and nevertheless deciding to ignore it
[Ref: Naresh Giri v. State of M.P., (2008) 1 SCC 791].

sentences.text: 12. If the statement is made that 'A' drove his car rashly and negligently, the said statement is not capable of objective verification by the Court or Tribunal as what is rash or negligence is an inference and a matter of opinion [Ref: Dias Jurisprudence, 5th Ed. p. 8].

For the objective verification by the Court or Tribunal, if 'A' was driving his car rashly and negligently, facts required to be proved on the basis of which the Court/Tribunal could reach to the inference and form an opinion that he was driving his car rashly and negligently.

sentences.text: Now coming to the issue, with respect to the rashness and/ or negligence of respondent no.1 in driving the offending vehicle the petitioner has deposed in his examination-in-chief Ex.PW1/A, as under:
"On the intervening night of 27/28.01.2019 (at about 12.30 midnight) the deponent was going on Eicher truck bearing no. DL 1 LAA-3446 (hereinafter referred to as aforesaid vehicle) as helper.
I was going in aforesaid vehicle from Delhi and was proceed (sic) towards Ashoka Fom Factory Mengi Nagla Faridpur Bareilly (Uttar Pradesh).

When we reached near Navadigya Jhada, Dev Sthan Bareilly (Uttar Pradesh) certainly a nilgai (blue bull) came in front of aforesaid vehicle and the driver/respondent no. 1, who was driving the aforesaid vehicle in high speed, rashly and negligently without caring for the rules of traffic cannot control the aforesaid vehicle and collided the aforesaid vehicle with truck parked on the side of the road.
As a result of forceful impact the injured sustained grievous."

14. The deposition of PW1 that 'the offending vehicle was being driven by respondent no.1 at a high speed, rashly and negligently without caring for the rules of traffic' was the opinion of PW1 and his Salim vs Sageer Ahamad on 8 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/181318002/
5 inference.
What is the high speed, depends upon the circumstances of the case.
What may be a high speed in a crowded market may not be high-speed in an open highway.

Nowhere in his deposition the petitioner PW1 has stated as to what was the exact or the approximate speed of the offending vehicle so that the Tribunal could have been able to assess if the speed at which the respondent no. 1 w a s d r i v i n g t h e o f f e n d i n g v e h i c l e c o u l d b e t e r m e d a s a r a s h a c t .

entities.text: Saleem v. Sageer Ahmad & Ors. Page 9 15
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: What is rash or negligent act is a matter of inference which is to be drawn on the basis of facts.
The petitioner merely saying that the respondent no.1/ driver of the offending vehicle was driving it rashly and negligently does not convey any fact to the Tribunal.

It is the Tribunal who is duty-bound to draw the inferences on the basis of facts which are to be proved by the petitioner if or if not the respondent no.1/ driver was driving the offending vehicle rashly and/ or negligently.

16. If the respondent no.1 violated any rules of the traffic which the petitioner/PW1 is alleging, then it would be PW1 who would be in a better position to state as to which rules of the traffic that the respondent no.1 violated.

The Tribunal is unable to draw any inference on the basis of what has been deposed to by PW1 in paragraph no.1 of his affidavit Ex.PW1/A with respect to the respondent no.1 being rash and negligent in driving the offending vehicle.

In the cross-examination of the petitioner,
the other respondents are supposed to contradict the facts and not the opinions of the petitioner whose opinion has not been sought by the Tribunal.
17. Moreover, there is nothing on record to indicate objectively that the petitioner/ PW1 was travelling on the offending vehicle on the intervening night of 27/28.01.2019.
If on the said date, the petitioner was travelling in the said vehicle then it has not been proved that the same was being driven by respondent no.1.
If the respondent no.1 was driving the offending vehicle, then the respondent no. 1 was driving the offending vehicle rashly or negligently.

If the respondent ______________________________________________________________________ MACT no. 195/2019; Saleem v. Sageer Ahmad & Ors. Page 10 no.1 was driving the offending vehicle rashly or negligently any accident was caused.
That if any accident was caused the petitioner received any injury in the said accident.

Keeping into consideration the relationship of the petitioner and respondent no. 1; they are the father and son, any admissions made by the respondent no. 1 in his written statement has to be carefully considered for proof of any fact being admitted by respondent no. 1.
18.
The GD entry Mark-C is dated 29/01/2019 recorded at 07:55 PM states about the chance happening of the accident on 28/01/2019 at about 12:30 a.m. with the offending vehicle.

As no FIR was lodged on the basis of the said GD entry, and no FIR could have been lodged on the basis of the said GD entry as the said GD entry did not complain about any offence being caused, therefore there is no independent verification of the facts by the police department which have been stated in GD entry Mark-C.
19.

Going with the deposition of the petitioner after the petitioner was injured in the accident involving the offending vehicle which was being driven by respondent no.1, the petitioner was Salim vs Sageer Ahamad on 8 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/181318002/
6 initially admitted in Leelawati Orthopaedic Center, near Soad Dharam Kanta, Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh.

20. If the case of the petitioner was that he had received the injuries in a road traffic accident then the preparation of MLC of the injured by the Hospital where the petitioner went for his treatment was mandatory as getting injury in road traffic accident is a medico-legal case and in the case of s u c h n a t u r e t h e d o c t o r s a r e u n d e r o b l i g a t i o n t o ______________________________________________________________________ MACT no. 195/2019; Saleem v. Sageer Ahmad & Ors. Page 11 prepare medico-legal certificate (MLC).
21.

sentences.text: In the present case, the petitioner has not proved even a single document of the Hospital namely Leelawati Orthopedics Center, where the petitioner was immediately taken after his accident on 27/28.01.2019.

There could be many possibilities why the petitioner has not proved any documents of Leelawati Orthopedics Center and one of the possibilities could be that the petitioner did not inform the doctor at Leelawati Orthopedics Center that he had received the injuries in a road traffic accident.

Anyway, adverse inference has to be drawn against the petitioner that had the petitioner produced and proved the relevant documents from Leelawati Orthopedics Center that would have gone against the interest of the petitioner.

22. The registration of FIR with respect to road accident in which anyone might have received accident is not sine-qua-non for the maintainability of claim petition under section 166 of Motor Vehicles Act but in that situation when no FIR has been registered, it becomes very onerous for the petitioner to prove the involvement of the offending vehicle in the alleged accident as if there is registration of FIR with respect to rash and negligent driving of the motor vehicle during the accident and independent agency investigates into the facts and circumstances of the case and if the charge-sheet is filed against the driver of the offending vehicle, who might have caused the accident,
it lends supports to the petitioner in making it much easier for the petitioner to prove certain material facts.

In the present case, as there was no registration of FIR with respect to the alleged ______________________________________________________________________ MACT no. 195/2019; Saleem v. Sageer Ahmad & Ors. Page 12 accident in which the petitioner received injuries, many facts even on the balance of probability e.g. the involvement of the offending vehicle in the accident, has not been proved by the petitioner.

23. As per the case of the petitioner, he was travelling in the offending vehicle as a helper and as per the insurance policy of the offending vehicle, the helper was not covered under the insurance policy.

When on this aspect, the clarification was sought by learned counsel for the petitioner, he tried to argue that the helper and the cleaner are one and the same with reference to a transport/ goods carriage vehicle.

This Tribunal does not find the said argument of the learned counsel for the petitioner to be convincing as in insurance parlance, the terms 'cleaner' and 'helper' has definite connotations and the word the 'cleaner' does not mean the 'helper' or vice versa.

24. In the present case, for the reasons best-known to the petitioner and/ or drafting counsel who drafted the claim petition under section 166 of Motor Vehicles Act, everywhere the petitioner has Salim vs Sageer Ahamad on 8 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/181318002/
7 been referred to as the 'helper' and not only that even the deposition is being led by the petitioner stating himself as 'helper' in his affidavit Ex.PW1/A and the 'helper' by the insurance policy of the offending vehicle is not covered.

25. In the light of discussion herein above, the Tribunal is of the opinion that even on the balance of probability, the petitioner has failed to prove any of the material facts as stipulated in the issue under discussion.
Accordingly, issue no.1 is decided in favour of the respondents and against the petitioner.

sentences.text: Whether the petitioner is entitled to compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom?
As the issue no.1 has been decided against the petitioner, the petitioner is not entitled for any compensation.
Accordingly, issue no.2 is decided against the petitioner and in favour of the respondents.
27. As both the substantive issues have been decided against the petitioner, the petitioner is not entitled to any relief for compensation from this Tribunal.
28. The claim petition is, accordingly, dismissed.

For the objective verification by the Court or Tribunal, if 'A' was driving his car rashly and negligently, facts required to be proved on the basis of which the Court/Tribunal could reach to the inference and form an opinion that he was driving his car rashly and negligently.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
It is settled proposition of law that in an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine-qua-non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of the preponderance of probabilities.
Holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.
Reference may be made to the judgments titled as New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v.
Sakshi Bhutani & Others., MAC APP. No. 550/2011 decided on 02.07.2012, Bimla Devi & Others v.
Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Others (2009) 13 SC 530, Parmeshwari v. Amirchand ______________________________________________________________________ MACT no. 195/2019; Saleem v. Sageer Ahmad & Ors. Page 6 & Others 2011 (1) SCR 1096 & Mangla Ram v. Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. & Others 2018, Law Suit (SC) 303.
9.
'Negligence' is failure to take proper care which a reasonable man would have taken under the circumstances.
What amounts to negligence depends on the facts of each particular case.
It may consist in omitting to do something which ought to be done or in doing something which ought to be done either in a different manner or not at all.
Where there is no duty to exercise care, negligence in the popular sense has no legal consequence.
Where there is a duty to exercise care, reasonable care must be taken to avoid acts or omissions which can be reasonably foreseen to be likely to cause physical injury to persons or property.
The degree of care required in the particular case depends on the surrounding circumstances, and may vary according to the amount of the risk to be encountered and to the magnitude of the prospective injury.
The duty of care is owed only to those persons who are in the area of foreseeable danger; the fact that the act of the defendant violated his duty of care to a third person does not enable the plaintiff who is also injured by the same act to claim unless he is also within the area of foreseeable danger.
What is rash or negligent act is a matter of inference which is to be drawn on the basis of facts.
The petitioner merely saying that the respondent no.1/ driver of the offending vehicle was driving it rashly and negligently does not convey any fact to the Tribunal.
It is the Tribunal who is duty-bound to draw the inferences on the basis of facts which are to be proved by the petitioner if or if not the respondent no.1/ driver was driving the offending vehicle rashly and/ or negligently.
